title: Use suboptimal sensitivities to expose weak mechanics in training
summary: A deliberately suboptimal sensitivity can make hidden movement weaknesses more visible, helping isolate arm speed, wrist fine control, or fingertip precision during training.
why: Using an unusual sensitivity can make a neglected muscle group or coordination pattern impossible to hide behind a comfortable default.
A very slow sens highlights arm speed and range demands, while a very fast sens makes fine wrist or fingertip control more visible.
actions: Use a slower-than-normal block on long-flick or wide-angle work if you want to stress arm speed and follow-through.
Use a faster-than-normal block on precision work if you want to expose fine wrist and fingertip control issues.
Keep these blocks intentional and time-boxed, then carry the cleaned-up movement back to your main sensitivity.
avoid: Do not turn every session into random sensitivity roulette.
Avoid judging the training block only by score if the real goal is isolating a mechanical weakness.

drills.reason: A slower setting exposes whether the arm can cover long distances quickly and cleanly.

evidence.claim: Deliberately mismatching sensitivity to the task can be used as a training tool to isolate different mechanical weaknesses.
evidence.excerpt: Suboptimal sensitivities can highlight arm speed, wrist control, and other movement limitations more clearly than the normal setting.
